Physics is the study of nature and how the universe behaves

Involves the study of matter and its motion through space and time, along with related concepts like energy and force

The boundary between physics and other sciences is not always clear -- basic laws of physics apply to all things

What differentiates physics from biology for example - while theores that describe living things ultimately result
from the fundamental laws of physics, they cannot easily be rigorously derived from physical principles

Matter

Theory

An explanation for patterns in nature that is supported by scientific evidence
and verified

More complex and dynamic, describing an entire group of related phenomena,
rather than a single observable point of fact

Whereas a law is a postulate that forms the foundation of the scientific method,
a theory is the end result of that process

Concise descriptions of the universe around us

Not explanations but statements of underlying rules

Intrinsic to the Universe, not created or changed by humans

The cornerstone for discovering natural laws is observation

Can never be known with absolute certainty (can't experiment
every possible scenario)

Valid until conterexample is observed

Representation of something often too difficult or impossible to display directly

While a models design is justifed using experimental info, it is only accurate
under limited situations

Ex: the planetary model of the atom

Anything that has mass and volume

The Celestial Sphere

Lying on your back at night, you get the impression that the sky is a great sphere that turns around you

The stars, like the sun and the moon, rise in the East and set in the West

On a single night, everything moves fixed relative to the stars (even planets, which have significant motions of their own

A line extended through the poles creates the celestial poles

The sky appears to turn in opposite directions around each

The apparent motion of the celestial sphere depends on your latitude

At the poles, an observer sees only half the sky, with no rising or setting

At the equator, an observer sees all stars exactly half the time in a 24 hr period

At latitudes in between (ex 38 degrees), the south celestial pole is 38 degrees below the horizon,
all stars within 38 degrees of the North Pole do not set, they are always above the horizon

Circumpolar zone

Stars within 38 degrees of South Celestial pole never rise

Polaris

Astronomers measure distances in the night sky using angles

The dome of the sky contains 180 degrees from horizon to horizon

Two stars 18 degrees apart span 1/10th the dome

The full Moon is about half a degree across (width of your smallest finger at arms length)

Area of sky in which stars do not set, sky revolves around the associated celestial pole

Closest to north celestial pole, moves the least

Played significant role in Native American mythology, called the fastener of the sky

Rising and Setting of the Sun

On a given day, we think of the Sun as being located at some position on the celestial sphere

Ancients were aware the Sun does more than just rise and set, it changes position gradually on the celestial sphere

Moves about 1 degree to the east relative to the stars

Takes a period of 1 year to make a full circle

The Ecliptic

As months go by, we look at sun from different places in our orbit, and see it projected against
different stars in the background

After a year, the sun appears to have completed one circuit of the skay along the ecliptic

Fixed and Wandering Stars

Not only sun that moves relative to stars - the Moon and visible plants (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranaus (barely)),
all change positions slowly from day to day

All rise and set, but unlike the Sun, have independent motions among the stars, superimposed on rotation of the celestial sphere

Greeks designated them planets, - wandering stars, as opposed to fixed

Designated the week to the seven moving objects

The individual paths of the Moon and planets all lie close to the ecliptic, though not exactly on it

This is because paths of the planets about sun and moon about earth are all in nearly the same plane

The planets, sun and Moon are always found in the sky in a narrow 18 degree wide belt, known as the Zodiac (from zoo - animal)

The planets motion in the sky is a combination of their actual motion plus the motion of Earth around the sun,
creating complex paths

Constelations

With no clouds and a flat backdrop, we could see about 3000 stars unaided

Astronomers use the term constellation to mean one of 88 sections into which we divide the sky

Modern boundaries are imaginary lines running north-south and east-west

Where possible, constellations are named after the Greek star pattern lying within it (ex Orion), also called asterism

Ex: Big Dipper is an asterism within the constellation of Ursa Major, the Big Bear

Greeks likely named asterisms in honor of characters and fit as best they could, instead of strictly resemblance

Significant Figures

Order of Magnitude

Defined as a measurement of physical quantity of distance

Many qualitative observations fundamental to physics are described using
or dependent on length -- distance between objects, rate of travel, force exerted on

The basic unit of length in the SI is the meter

Meter

The distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second

All lengths measured in terms of meter, multiples devised around the number 10

Mass, specifically inertial mass, is a quantitative measure of an objects
resistance to acceleration

It is an intrinsic property of an object and does not change because of environment

The SI unit of mass is the kilogram

Defined in relation to the Prototype kilogram, only SI unit defined by an artifact

Four of the seven base units in the SI system are defined relative to the kilogram

Weight is often given in kilograms -- this is the non SI unit known as kilogram force

Mass may be re-definied in terms of the Planck constant

One of the seven fundamental physical quantities in the International System of Units

Used to defined other quantities, such as velocit or acceleration

Defined in the past by astronomical phenomena or mean solar day, but today definied in terms
of radiation emitted by cesium atoms

Some units widely umsed but not part of SI include the minute, hour, day, liter, degree, minute, second (angles)

Units of measurement for the same quantity can be converted using conversion factors

Factor-label method

Sequential application of conversion factors expressed as fractions
and arranged so that any dimensional unit appearing in both numerator
and denominator can be cancelled out until only desired unit is obtained

Can only convert between units that have a constant ratio that can be multiplied

Cannot be used between units that have a displacement or difference factor (ex converting Celsius to Fahrenheit

The class of scale of any amount in which each class contains values of a fixed ratio to the class preceding it

Most commonly the amount scaled is 10, and the scale is the exponent applied to this amount

Differences can be measured on the log scale

Generaly used to make approximate comparisons and reflect large differences

It is important that estimates be at lease in the right ballpark, ex within an order of magnitude
of the value in question

Dimensional Analysis

Any physical quantity can be expressed as a product of a combination of the basic physical dimensions

Dimensional analysis is the practice of checking relations between physical quantities by identifying their
dimensions.

The dimension of any physical quantity is the combination of the basic physical dimensions that compose it;
indicates how it relates to the seven basic quantities

Seven Basic Quantitites

[M] Mass

[L] Length

[T] Time

[A] Current

[K] Temperature

[mol] Amount of a Substance

[cd] Luminous Intensity

Square brackets are often used to represent the
dimension of an individual basic quantity

Ex: Speed has a dimension of 1 in length and -1 in time:

SI Base Quantities

Derived Dimensions

The dimensions of derived quantitites may include multiple individual basic quantitites

Ex: Force - defined as Mass * acceleration

The dimension of acceleration is itself a derived quantity (ratio of velocity and time)

Velocity is in turn a derived quantity - the ratio of length and time

Dimensional Conversion

To convert between dimensions, find the conversion factor

Where n represents amount per u dimensions

You can then use ratios to figure out the conversion

Free Body Diagram

Visually represents a physics problem using geometry and vectors

Trigonometry is used to solve for the x and y components of forces and objects

Bodies are modeled in one of three ways:

As a particle - used when any turning effects are zero or have zero interest

A force on a particle is a bound vector

Rigid extended -- stresses and strains are of no interest, but turning effects are

A force arrow should lie along the line of force, where where along the line is irrelevant

A force on an extended rigid body is a sliding vector

Non-rigid extended -- the point of application of a force becomes crucial and has to be indicated

A force on a non-rigid body is a bound vector

Some engineers use the tail of the arrow to indicate the point of application, others use the tip

Making a diagram

Include the body -- usually sketched in a schematic way depending on the body and what questions
are to be answered

If rotation and torque are in consideration, and indication of size and shape of the body is needed

Include external forces -- indicated by labelled arrows

In a fully solved problem, a force arrow is capable of indicating the direction, magnitude, and point of application

Forces can be friction, gravity, normal force, drag, tension, etc

Do not show bodies other than the body of interest

Do not show forces exerted by the body

Do not include internal forces acting on various parts of the body by other parts of the body

Velocity or acceleration is left out

Astronomy around the World

Ancient Babylonian, Assyrian and Egyptian astronomers knew the approximate length of the year

Egyptians had 365 day year, tracked Sirius in the predawn sky - yearly cycle corresponded with the flooding of the Nile

Chinese figured out length of the year around same time as Egyptians, recorded meteors, comets, dark spots on the Sun

Keopt careful records of guest stars (stars too faint that suddenly flared up - supernovae)

Mayans kept sophisticated calendar based on Venus

Polynesians navigated with the stars

In Britain, ancient people used stones to keep track of motions of Sun and Moon

Early Greek and Roman Cosmology

The word cosmology is of Greek Origin

Ancient Greeks knew of a spherical Earth 2500 years ago

Stemmed from time of Pythagoras -- belief in perfect forms (circles & spheres),
such as the Moon

Aristotle (384-322 BC) (tutor of Alex the Great) summarized many ideas of his day

Described progression of Moon's phases as caused by seeing different sunlit portions
as month progressed

Knew Sun had to be farther away from Earth than the moon (eclipses)

Cited shadow of earth on moon during an eclipse as evidence of sphere Earth

Only sphere always casts round shadow - disk would appear flat or line at some points

Also noted travelers moving South observe stars not visible farther north, and height of north star
decreases as moving south

Aristarchus of Samos (310-230BC) even suggested that Earth was moving around sun, but idea
was rejected -- though must observe different stars at different points in orbit if that was the case,
stars would shift relative to each other (stellar parallax)

Meant stars were tremendously far away, an enormous cosmos that was too much of a leap of imagination
for the greeks

Measurement of Earth by Eratosthenes

Eratosthenes (276 - 194) a greek living in Alexandria used geometric method to measure size of earth through observations of the Sun

Sun is so distant (150 mil km) that its rays strike our planet along essentially parallel lines

Eratosthenes was told on solstice at Syene, Egypt (moder day Aswan), sunlight
struck the bottom of a vertical well at Noon (directly overhead)

A shadow at the same date in Alexandria cast a shadow of angle 1/50th of a circle (7 degrees)

Eratosthenes surmised the distance between Syrene and Alexandria must be 1/50th of the circumferance of Earth

Hipparchus and Precession

Hipparchus was possibly greatest astronomer of antiquity

Born in Nicaea (modern day Turkey)

Built observatory on island of Rhodes around 150 BC

Measured position of objects in sky, compiling a star catelog with about 850 entries

Designated celestial coordinates for each star

Divided stars in apparent magnitudes according to brightness

Observed and compared data with older observations -- deduced that position of the
north celestial pole had altered over previous century and half

Deduced that this motion was continuously happening -- precession

Precession of earths top axis describes the shape of a cone as earth's gravity tries to topple

The Earths bulge at equator being pulled by Sun and Moon causes the precessional wobble

Takes 26,000 years to complete one circle

Polaris is closest to north celestial pole today (closest point around 2100), the star
Vega in constellation of Lyra with be North star in 14,000 years

Ptolemy's Model of the Solar System

Claudius Ptolemy - last great astronomer of the Roman Era

Lived in Alexandria about 140 AD

Wrote compilation of astronomical knowledge, known by its Arabic name Almagest

It is one of the main sources of information about the work of Hipparchus and other Greek astronomers

Ptolemy's most important work was creating a geometric system that predicted the positions of the planets
for any desired date and time

Used data compiled by Hipparchus as well as his own observations

Constructed a model to explain retrograge motion using only circles

Remained in use for over 1000 years until time of Copernicus

Used a system of epicycles revolving around Earth on a circle called the deferent

Monomers and Polymers

Most biological macromolecules are polymers

Polymers are constructed by linking many smaller molecules, called monomers

Typically all the monomers in a polymer tend to be the same or very similar, linked over and over again to build
up the larger macromolecule

Ex: regular table sugar (the disaccharide sucrose, a polymer) is formed by the
monosaccharaides fructose and glucose (which are monomers)

Stringing further carbohydrate monomers creates a polysaccharide like starch

Biological macromolecules all contain carbon in ring
or chain form (meaning they're classified as organic molecules)

Also contain hydrogen and oxygen, nitrogen and additional minor elements

Biological macromolecules perform wide array of functions, make up
most of a cells dry mass

Molecular units in biomacromolecules are connected to each other by strong covalent bonds

Dehydration Synthesis

Only lipids are not made up of monomers (units with similar composition and size)

Monomers combine via covalent bonds to form larger molecules, in doing so release water molecules as byproducts

This type of reaction known as dehydration synthesis

Also considered to be a condensation reaction since two molecules are condensed into one large molecule
with the loss of one smaller molecule

In dehydration synthesis reactions between two un-ionized monomers (ex monosacchardie sugars), the hydrogen of one monomer
combines with the hydroxyl group of another monomer

The removal of hydrogen and hydroxyl allows the monomers to share electrons and form a covalent bond

When the monomers are ionized (such as amino acids
in an aqueous environment like cytoplasm), the two
hydrogens from + charged end of one monomer are
combined with an oxygen from - charged end of other
monomer, again forming water

In dehydration synthesis between two amino acids (ionized in
aqueous envionrments like the cell) an oxygen from first forms
with two hydrogens, creating covalent bond to form a
dipeptide

As additional monomers join via multiple dehyd synth reactions, chain of repeating monomers begins to form a polymer

Polymers can configure in many combinations, giving rise to diverse group of macromolecules

3/4 macromolucles (complex carbs, nucleic acids, proteins) are formed by dehydration synthesis

Complex carbs from monosaccharides, nucleic acids from mononucleotides, proteins from amino acids

Starches, cellulose, glycogen are all formed by glucose monomers -- the manner by which they join --
specifically the locations of the covalent bonds, orientation (stereochemistry) of the bonds, results in
different polysaccharides with different properties and functions

In nucleic acids and proteins, the location and stereochemistry of covalent linkages
connecting monomers (five different monomers in nuceic acids (A,G,C,T, and U mononucleotides,
21 different amino acid monomers in proteins), are combined in a huge variety of sequences

Each protein or nucleic acid with a different sequence is a different molecule

Hydrolysis

Result in the breakdown of polymers into monomers by using a water molecule
and an enzymatic catalyst

If components are un-ionized, one part gains a hydrogen atom (H-) and the other
gains a hydroxyl group (OH-) from a split water molecule

This is what happens when monosaccharides are release from complex carbs

If components are ionized after the split, one part gains two hydrogen atoms
and a positive charge, the other part gains an oxygen atom and a negative charge

This is what happens when amino acids are released from protein chains via hydrolysis

Ex dipeptide broken down to form two ionized amino acids

Dehydration and hydrolysis reactions are chemical reactions that are catalyzed
by specific enzymes

Dehydration reactions involve formation of new bonds, requiring energy, while
hydrolysis reactions break bonds and release energy

In our bodies, food is hydrolyzed into smaller molecules by catalytic enzymes in the
digestive tract, allowing for easy absorption of nutrients by cells in intestine

Each macromolecule is broken down by specific enzyme

Carbs are broken down by amylase, sucrase, lactase, or maltase

Proteins are broken down by trypsin, pepsin, peptidase, and others

Lipids are broken down by lipases

Once smaller metabolites are absorbed by cells, they are further broken down by other enzymes

The breakdown provides energy for cellular activites

Carbohydrates are classified into three subtypes -- monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides

Monosaccharides are simple sugars made up of three to seven carbons, can exist as a linear chain or as ring-shaped molecules

Glucose, galactose, and fructose are monosaccharide isomers, all have same chemical formula but differ
structurally and chemically

Ancient peoples regarded planets & stars as representatives / symbols of the gods & forces

Connected to life & death understanding of the actions of the gods

Planets (wander through sky) had special significance

Ex Greece - planets had names of gods and were credited with having the same powers and influences
as the gods whose names they bore

Beginnings of Astrology

Astrology began in Babylonia about 2.5 millenia ago

Used their knowledge of astronomy to guide their rulers

When Babylonian culture was absorbed by the Greeks, astrology gradually came to influence the entire Western world
and eventually spread to Asia

By 2nd Century CE Greeks had idea that astrology influenced every individual

Natal astrology (configuration at birth) reached its peak with Ptolemy - compiled the Tetrabiblos - bible of

The Laws of Planetary Motion

Tycho Brahe

Born 3 years after Copernicus' De Revolutionibus

Danish nobility

Made significant observations, including of supernova

Established astronomical observatory on North Sea island of Hven

Last and greatest pre-telescopic observers

Made continuous record of the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets for
almost 20 years

Noted that positions of the planets varied from those in published tables
based on the work of Ptolemy

Couldn't develop a model for variances, fell out of government favor, moved
to Prague and became court astronomer to Emperor Rudolf of Bohemia

Found able young mathmetician, Johannes Kepler, to help analyze his data

Johannes Kepler

Born to a poor family in German Province of Wurttemberg

Lived life amid turmoil of the Thirty Years War

Studied in Tubingen

Learned principles of Copernican system and became converted to heliocentric hypothesis

Studied under Brahe, who was reluctant to provide material

Brahe died in 1601, Keppler gets possession of records

Developed series of principles, known as Kepler's three laws, described planets
paths through space

First published in 1609 in The New Astronomy

The First Two Laws of Planetary Motion

The path of an object through space is called its orbit

Kepler initially assumed orbits to be circles, but this was inconsistent with Brahe's observations

Working with data for Mars, he discovered that the orbit of that planet had the shape of an ellipse

After a circle, ellipses are the simplest kind of closed curve (conic sections)

Sum of the distance from two points (foci) inside an ellipse is always the same

To draw an ellipse, wrap ends of a loop around to tacks

Widest diameter of ellipse is its major axis -- half the distance is the semimajor axis,
which is usually used to specify size of the ellipse

Ex: the semimajor axis of the orbit of Mars (its average distance from the Sun) is 228 million kilometers

Ellipse with eccentricity of 0 (tacks in same spot) is a circle, maximum excentricity is 1.0 (flat)

Kepler found Mars had elliptical orbit, with Sun at one focus (other focus empty) with eccentricity of 0.1

Kepler's second law deals with the speed each planet moves along its ellipse (orbital speed)

Found that planets speed up as they come closer to the Sun and slows down as it pulls away

Expressed this relationship by imagining the Sun and Mars as connected by straight, elastic line

Kepler found that in equal intervals of time, the areas swept out in space by an imaginary line are always equal

Kepler's Third Law

Kepler wanted to understand why the orbits were spaced as they are and to find a mathematical pattern in their movements (harmony of the spheres)

Worked to discover mathematical relationships governing planetary spacing and the time it took each planet to go around the Sun

In 1619 he discovered a basic relationship to relate planets' orbits to their relative distances from the Sun

We defined a planets orbital period (P) as the time it takes to travel once around the Sun

Kepler's third law states that a planet's orbital period squared is proportional to the semimajor axis of its orbit cubed

When P is measured in years and a is expressed in astronomical units (AU), the two sides of the formula are equal

One AU is the average distance between Earth and the Sun (~ 1.5 x 10^8 km)

Kepler's third law provides a means for calculating their relative distances from the Sun from the time they take to orbit

Newton's Great Synthesis

Newton - born in Lincolnshire, England, the year after Galileo's death

Contemporaries in Englyand (Trinity, Cambridge) architect Christopher Wren,
Authors Aphra Behn, Daniel Defoe, composer G.F. Handel

Wrote and published Philosophiae Principia Mathematica (The Principia) after urging of Edmund Halley

Proposed three laws of motion

Newton's Laws of Motion

First Law

Second Law

Third Law

Interpretation of Newton's Laws

The First law is a restatement of one of Galileo's discoveries called the conservation of momentum

In the absence of any outside influence, there is a measure of a body's motion, called its momentum, that remains unchanged

Momentum - depends on three things - speed, direction, and mass

The term velocity is used to describe the speed and direction of motion

Momentum can then be defined as an object's mass times its velocity

The momentum of a body can change only under the action of an outside influence

Newton's second law expresses force in terms of its ability to change momentum with time

A force (push or pull) has both size and direction - when applied to a body, momentum changes in the
direction of the applied force

A force is required to change either the speed or the direction of a body, or both

The rate of change in an object's velocity is called acceleration -- Newton showed that the acceleration of a
body was proportional to hte force being applied to it

How much a force will accelerate an object is determined by its mass

Newton's third law gives us a way to define mass -- any change within the system must be balanced by another change
that is equal and opposite so that the momentum of the entire system is not changed

This means forces in nature do not occur alone -- there is always a pair of forces that are equal and opposite

Mass, Volume, and Density

Mass - measure of the amount of a material within an object

Volume - the physical space it occupies (cubic units)

Density -- mass / volume (ex grams per cubic cm)

Angular Momentum

Measure of the rotation of a body as it revolves around some fixed point (ex planet around sun)

Defined as the product of its mass, velocity, and distance from the fixed point around which it revolves

If these quantities remain constant (constant velocity at fixed distance) - then the angular momentum
is also constant

Kepler's second law is a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum

As planet approaches the Sun and distance to spin center decreases, the planet speeds up to conserve the
angular momentum and vice versa

Speed & Velocity

Velocity

A vector quantity denoting rate of change of position with respect to time

Or - speed with a directional component

Speed is scalar

Average speed = distance traveled over total time

Average velocity = change in position (displacement) over total time

SI unit for velocit is meters per second (m/s)

Instantaneous Velocity

Typically, motions is not constance (velocity or speed)

Results in a curvy line if graphed in small segments

Since velocity is constantly changing, we can estimate velocity by looking at instantaneous velocity

Instaneous velocity - ex how many meters object would travel at a specific moment

Defined by the slope of the line tangent to the curve at that point

This is equivalent to finding the first derivative

Acceleration

Acceleration is the rate at which the velocity of a body changes with time

Vector quantity with both magnitude and direction

SI unit of acceleration is the meter per second squared

Points in the same direction as the change in velocity, though may not
always be in the direction of motion (ex object slows down or decelerates,
acceleration is in the opposite direction of motion

Motion with Constant Acceleration

An object experiencing constant acceleration has a velocity that increases or decreases by an equal amount for any constant period of time

Accleration can be derived easily from basic kinematic principles

It is defined as the first time derivative of velocity (the second derivative of position with respect to time)

Assuming accleration to be constant does not limit the situations we can study and doesn't degrade the accuracy of our treatment

In a great number of situations, acceleration is constant, and when it is not, we can either consider it in separate parts of constant acceleration
or use an average acceleration over a period of time

Kinematic Equations

Relate displacement, initial velociy, final velocity, acceleration, and time

Problem-solving for Basic Kinematics

Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation

Newton's laws of motion state that objects in motion will continue moving uniformly in a straight line unless acted on by a force

Since planets move in ellipses, Newton proposed a force must be bending their paths (gravity)

In Newton's time, gravity was associated with Earth alone - Newton's insight was that Earth's gravity might extend as far as the Moon
and produce the force required to curve the Moon's path

Further hypothesized that gravity is not limited to Earth, but that there is a general force of attraction between all material bodies

Therefore the attractive force between Sun and planets would keep them in orbit (remarkable insight in Newton's time)

A mathematical description of gravity had to match orbits described by Kepler and falling bodies on Earth observed by Galileo

To deal with this problem, Newton invented Calculus

Newton concluded that gravitational attraction must be proportional to their masses

Objects at the surface of the Earth (one Earth-radius from center) are observed to accelerate downward at 9.8 m/s^2

The moon is 60 Earth radii away, acceleration is (1/60)^2 less, or 3600 times less), about 0.00272 m/s^2

Gravity is a built-in property of mass - whenever there are masses in the universe, they will interact via the force of gravity

Newton's law also implies that gravity never becomes zero -- continues to act to some degree no matter the distance

Orbital Motion & Mass

Knowing that gravity is the force attracting objects to sun allowed Newton to rethink Kepler's third law

Showed that it can be stated as:

In the case of the sun, the suns mass is 1, and the planets mass is a negligibly small factor,
meaning that their sum is close to 1.

There are many other situations in astronomy where we do need to include the two mass terms,
such as when two stars or galaxies orbit eachother

Including mass terms also allows us to use the formula -- if we can measure the motions
(distances and orbital periods) of objects acting under mutual gravity, then we can deduce their masses

Orbits in the Solar System

An orbit of any object, once determined, allows the future positions of the object to be calculated

The point where a planet is closest to the Sun (helios - Greek) and moves the fastest is called the perihelion

Aphelion - the place where it is farthest away and moves most slowly

For the Moon or a satellite orbiting Earth, the corresponding terms are perigee and apogee

Orbits of the Planets

All of the planets have orbits of rather low eccentricity

Mercury is the most eccentric (0.21), the rest have eccentricities smaller than 0.1

Fortunately Mars has an above average eccentricity -- allowing Kepler to deduce its elliptical shape

The planetary orbits are also confined close to a common plane - near the plane of Earth's orbit (the ecliptic)

Pluto's orbit is inclined about 17 degrees to the ecliptic, dwarf planet Eris by 44 degrees

All major planets lie within 10 degrees of the ecliptic

Orbits of Asteroids and Comets

Both asteroids and comets are believed to be small chunks of material left over from the formation process of the solar system

Asteroids have orbits with smaller semimajor axes than do comets in general

The majority of asteroids lie between 2.2 and 3.3 AU, in the region known as the asteroid belt

Largest memeber of the asteroid belt is Ceres

Lie in between orbits of Mars and Jupiter -- because these two planets are so far apart stable orbits of small bodies can exist between them

Motions of Satellites & Spacecraft

Sputnik - lauched by Soviet Union on Oct 4 1957

Once a satelite is in orbit, its behavior is no different from a natural satellite

If it is high enough to be free of atmospheric friction, it will remain in orbit forever

The speed needed for an object to fall around Earth in a complete circle (orbit) is 8 km / s (17,500 mph)

Each year more than 50 new satellites are launched, most into low Earth orbit (requires minimum launch energy)

At orbital speed of 8 km/s, they circle the pplanet in about 90 minutes

Some very low Earth orbits are not indefinitely stable due to frictional drag from atmosphere (atmosphere swells from time to time)

Interplanetary Spacecraft

To escape Earth's orbit, a craft must achieve escapee speed - 11 km/s (25k mph)

After this, they coast to their targets, with minor trajectory adjustments provided by small thrusters

In planetary flight, these craft follow orbits around the Sun that are modified only when passing near one of the planets

As they come closer to its target, spacecraft are deflected by a planets gravitational force into modified orbits,
gaining or losing energy

Spacecraft controllers use a planets gravity to redirect craft to a target (ex Voyager 2 on Jupiter flybys in 1979, Saturn 1980, Uranus 1986, Neptune 1989)

Galileo spacecraft (1989) flew past Venus & Earth to gain the energy required to reach its ultimate goal of orbiting Jupiter)

A return to Earth requires similar propulsive force in reverse

Gravity with More Than Two Bodies

All planets exert gravitational forcess upon one another

Interplanetary attractions cause slight variations from orbits

Motion under influence from two or more other bodies is complicated, can only be calculated properly with large computers

The Interactions of Many Bodies

Ex - cluster of 1k stars orbiting common center (star cluster) - knowing the position of each star, can calculate combined graviational force of entire group on any one member

Can therefore find how it will accelerate, how it will move (with initial velocity)

However, other stars are also moving, and thus changing the effect on the first star - therefore must simultaneously calculate the acceleration of each star
produced by the combination of the gravitational attractions of all the others

Such calculations have been carried out with clusters of stars up to a million members

Within the solar system, additional influences of other bodies are very small in comparison with dominant gravitational attraction of the Sun

Under such circumstances, it is possible to treat effects of small bodies as perturbations

18th and 19th century mathmeticians developed many elegant techniques for calculating perturbations, allowing them to predict positions of the planets

Such calculations led to the discovery of a new planet in 1846

The Discovery of Neptune

Discovery of Neptune was a high point in the development of gravitational theory

1781 - William Herschel - musician and amateur astronomer, accidentally discovered Uranus

Uranus had been observed a century before, but wasn't recognized as planet

By 1790, an orbit had been calculated for Uranus using observations of its motion, however, it was found that Uranus didnt' move in a way that fit earlier observation made in 1690

By 1840, the discrepancy between the positions observed and those predicted by its computed orbit amounted to about 0.03 degrees -
barely discernable to the eye but larger than the probable errors in the calculations

1843 - John Couch Adams - mathematical analysis of irregularities to see if they were produced by pull of unknown planet, more distant than Uranus, then determined the mass and orbit it
had to have to account for the departures in Uranus' orbit

In October 1845, presented results to George Airy, British Astronomer, telling him where to find the new planet (correct to within 2 degrees)

Simultaneously, French mathematician Urbain Jean Joseph Le Verier worked on the same problem, results agreed within 1 degree

Earth & Sky

Locating Places on Earth

Earth's rotation defines the four directions - poles by axis of rotation,
east is the direction toward which Earth rotates, west the opposite

These directions are well defined, except for on the poles

A meridian is a great circle passing through poles -- any point on Earth
has a meridian passing through it

Greenwich, England - longitude 0 - site of Royal Observatory, site of much
of the development of the method to measure longitude at sea

Latitidue is the number of degrees of arc you are away from the equator
along your meridian

Locating Places in the Sky

Positions in the sky are measured similarly to those on Earth

Coordinates are called declination and righ ascension

Declination is measured much as latitude - from celestial equator

Points of rotation are north and south celestial pole - halfway in between is the celestial equator

Right ascension is like longitude, except the abritrary 0 point is the vernal equinox

The Turning Earth

Stars rise and set each night

19th Century - French physicist Jean Focault provided unambigous demonstration of Earth's rotation

Suspended 60m pendulum with mass of 25kg from dome of the Pantheon in Paris

The Seasons

The Earth's distance from the sun only varies by about 3%

At summer solstice, sun shines most directly upon the Norther Hemisphere, appearing about 23 degree north of the equator,
passing through the zenith of places on Earth that are 23 degrees N latatiude (near Hawaii)

The latitude where the Sun can appear at the zenith at noon on the first day of summer is the Tropic of Cancer

Real World Effects

Atmosphere has effect of allowing us to see a little way over the horizon through refraction

Atmosphere scatters light, providing twilight illumination when Sun is below the horizon

Morning twilight begins when Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, and evening twilight as well (more than 18)

Atmospheric effects require small corrections - at equinoxes Sun appears to be above the horizon for a few minutes
longer than 12 hours

These effects are most dramatic at Earth's poles, where the Sun can be seen more than a week before it reaches the celestial equator

Keeping Time

The measurement of time is based on the rotation of the Earth

For most of history, time has been reckoned by positions of the Sun and stars in the sky

Only recently have mechanical and electronic clocks taken over this function

The Length of the Day

The most fundamental astornomical unit of time is the day, measured in terms of the rotation of Earth

There is more than one way to define the day:

Solar day - rotation period of the Earth with respect to the Sun (ex sunrise to sunrise

Sidereal day -- rotation period of Earth with respect to the stars

Solar day is slightly longer than a sidereal day - Earth not only turns but also moves along its path around the Sun

To complete a solar day, Earth must rotate an additional amount equal to 1/365th of a full turn (aprox 4 minutes)

Ordinary clocks are set to solar time (stars rise 4 minutes earlier each day), astornomers prefer sidereal time for planning observations

Apparent Solar Time

Apparent solar time is the time reckoned by the actual position of the Sun in the sky

Time as indicated by sundials, representing earliest measure of time by ancient civilizations

First half of day, sun hasn't yet reached meridiem (ante merdiem, am)

Apparent solar time seems simple, but isn't convenient to use -- exact length of apparent solar day varies slightly during the year

Eastward progress of the Sun in its annual journey around the sky is not uniform -- speed of the Earth varies slightly in its elliptical orbit

Also, Earth's axis of rotation is not perpendicular to the plane of its revolution -- thus solar time does not advance at a uniform rate

Mechanical clocks run at uniform rate

Mean Solar Time and Standard Time

Mean solar time -- based on the average value of the solar day over the course of the year

Contains exactly 24 hours

Still not convenient -- time of noon is different as you change your longitude

Until end of 19th century, every city and town kept its own local mean time -- with railroads and telegraph, need for standardization became evident

By 1900 most of world was using the system of 24 standardized global time zones, with local mean solar time
of a standard line of longitude running through middle of zone
